demographics.trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one

Threat.value: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place
Being superalert or watchful or on guard
Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame

issues.item: Threat from Strangers: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
issues.explanation: For trauma involving the unexpected death of a loved one, a specific sense of danger from strangers is hard to reconcile unless there is additional trauma history not represented here. The other threat items reflect generalized hypervigilance, but this item implies an interpersonal-danger context that is not supported by the trauma type or by any trigger, memory, appraisal, or strategy items.

issues.item: Scanning for Danger: I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger
issues.explanation: For trauma involving the unexpected death of a loved one, this threat profile is hard to reconcile clinically: all selected items imply persistent fear of immediate external physical danger, which fits assault/combat more than bereavement trauma. In isolation, bereavement-related PTSD can involve arousal, but a purely danger-scanning threat node without any accompanying memory, trigger, appraisal, or strategy content linking the threat to reminders of the loved one's death is not coherent here. This is also difficult to square with the formulation, which specifies no active edges; the threat items strongly imply linkage to triggers or trauma reminders, yet no such connected content is present.

vignette:
At 31, Linh Tran came to treatment looking exhausted in a way that seemed to live in her muscles as much as on her face. She was a Vietnamese American journalist, recently divorced, and she described the event that divided her life into a before and after as the sudden death of her younger brother, Minh. He had been 27 when he was killed in a late-night highway crash after driving home from a family dinner. Linh had been one of the last people to see him alive. She still remembered standing with him under the harsh yellow light outside the restaurant, both of them lingering beside their cars as siblings do, talking for a few extra minutes when they should already have left. She had told him to text when he got home. Instead, hours later, she was woken by repeated calls and then by her mother's voice, strained and broken, saying there had been an accident and that Minh was dead.

In the first days afterward, Linh moved through practical tasks with the sharpened focus she knew from breaking-news reporting. She spoke to relatives, helped with funeral arrangements, answered questions, and relayed information. But even in those early days she noticed that her body no longer settled. She would sit on her couch in the quiet of her apartment and feel as though something terrible were still in motion, as if catastrophe had not ended but only paused. She knew, rationally, that she was indoors, the door locked, the room still. Yet she could not relax. Her shoulders stayed lifted, her jaw clenched, her breathing shallow enough that she often realized she had been holding it. At night she would lie in bed listening for sounds in the hallway, in the street below, in neighboring apartments, alert to every shift in noise as though bad news might announce itself again.

Over the following months, that watchfulness threaded itself through her days. As a journalist, Linh worked in a busy newsroom where phones rang, police scanners murmured, editors called across desks, and breaking alerts flashed across multiple screens. She had once thrived in that atmosphere. Now she found herself constantly scanning it. If a phone rang sharply nearby, her head snapped up before anyone else's. If a colleague's tone changed while speaking to an editor, a pulse of dread went through her. She began monitoring her own phone obsessively, checking for missed calls, reading and rereading family group texts, keeping the volume high even in meetings because she was certain that if she missed one call, something irreversible would happen again. She told herself this was vigilance, responsibility, the sensible response to knowing how suddenly life could split open. But it meant she never felt off duty. Even on quieter assignments, seated in a safe office with people she knew well, her body behaved as if she were bracing for impact.

What was hardest for Linh was the intensity of feeling that could seize her without warning. Fear came first and fastest: a cold, immediate conviction that someone else she loved could die at any moment. Alongside it was horror, not abstract but tied to the fact of how abruptly Minh had vanished from an ordinary evening. Anger arrived too, hot and disorganizing, sometimes directed at the driver who hit him, sometimes at the randomness of it, sometimes at Minh for getting on the road at all. Guilt sat closest to her. She had come to replay their last conversation with punishing precision. She was certain she should have insisted he stay longer, or sleep at her place, or at least not drive so late. The fact that she could not know whether any of that would have changed the outcome did not soften the accusation in her own mind. What frightened her most was how quickly these feelings could flood her, as though she had no skin against them.

Her divorce, finalized not long before she sought help, had left her with even fewer places where she felt able to let down her guard. She said little to friends because she did not want to hear reassurances that felt false. At work she remained competent, but colleagues noticed she startled easily and stayed tense through entire shifts. She took on stories she could complete from the office rather than spending extra time out on assignment, telling herself she needed to be reachable. Her world had narrowed around readiness.

Linh finally sought therapy after a recent newsroom moment shook her. An editor called her name from across the room just as her phone lit up with her mother's number, and a surge of terror hit so strongly that she had to grip the edge of her desk. For several seconds she was unable to hear what anyone was saying. The call turned out to be ordinary, but she was left trembling and ashamed that safety no longer registered as safety to her. Sitting in the intake session, she said she was tired of living as if disaster were always one sound away. At the same time, she was afraid that if she stopped being so alert, she would be failing the people she had left. What she hoped for, cautiously, was not to forget Minh, but to be able to be in a room, at work or at home, and feel that she was actually there rather than waiting for the next call that would ruin everything.
